articles.title: Heat warning extended for San Diego County as some temps hit above 100 - NBC 7 San Diego

articles.full_text:
Heat alerts warning of dangerous weather conditions are in effect for each of San Diego County's climate zones through Thursday as a stifling heat wave peaks.
The heat warning has been extended through Thursday evening for San Diego's coasts and inland valleys, where dangerously high temperatures could be as much as 10-15 degrees above average.
Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7.
Inland temperatures reached triple digits again on Wednesday, while coastal temperatures reached 90s, according to NBC 7 Meteorologist Greg Bledsoe.
Gillespie Field airport in El Cajon unofficially hit 108 degrees just a little before 1 p.m. Wednesday, Bledsoe said.
San Diego County's mountains are under a heat advisory through Thursday at 8 p.m. Showers are still possible over the mountains each afternoon, but chances will drop as the week goes on.
Out in the boiling desert, an extreme heat warning is in effect through Friday at 8 p.m.
The weekend will continue to cool. We should also see more morning marine layer clouds, and cooler overnight temperatures. More seasonal temperatures will continue into next week.
Adding to the discomfort is excessively high humidity stemming from a mix of monsoonal moisture and heat rising from warmer-than-usual ocean temperatures, according to the National Weather Service. Much of the county continues to feel muggy and the mountains saw some afternoon thunderstorms this week.
Tropical storms hundreds of miles away, like the recent Hurricane Marie, can also increase humidity.
"The effects of Marie have faded but the monsoonal flow has returned. So, we’re not really getting much of a break from the humidity," Bledsoe said.
While some relief will come Thursday and Friday, lower humidity and cooler temperatures are not likely to come before next Sunday, according to the NWS.
SDG&E power outages
The heat is putting a strain on the power grid, leading to outages across San Diego. NBC 7’s Dave Summers reports.
The extreme heat also prompted San Diego Gas & Electric to carry out some unplanned outages across the county.
Within 24 hours between Tuesday and Wednesday, SDG&E had 29 unplanned outages.
A blackout struck at about 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, knocking out power to 8,719 SDG&E customers in Del Dios, Green Valley, the Lake Hodges vicinity, Poway, Rancho Bernardo, Rancho Penasquitos and San Pasqual, according to the utility.
Service was expected to be restored to the affected areas by late afternoon on Wednesday.
"Community members out there with this type of temperature, they’re going to start using the A/C a little bit more, fans, and that on top of appliances that they already use. That’s going to put strain on the grid," SDG&E spokesperson Humberto Gurmilan said.
San Diego Fire-Rescue Department responded to a power line down last night on Jamacha Road near Sacramento Avenue on Wednesday morning. Hundreds of people in the neighborhood were out of power till around 2 a.m.
Omar Osorio said he returned home after six hours in the hospital with stomach pain. His illness was aggravated by a night without air conditioning.
“My home it was super hot, no AC at all, it was really bad,” he said.
His neighbor David Orosco has six people total living under his roof. Many of them were sleepless in Spring Valley Tuesday night.
“Everybody was out here just trying to cool off, it was cooler outside then inside the house," Orosco said.
A Chula Vista power pole caught fire Tuesday night because of what appeared to be a power equipment malfunction.
The California Independent Operator coordinates the power grid to make sure electricity supply matches customer demand in real time across 80% of California.
Until then, SDG&E recommends conserving energy by minimizing the use of appliances during peak hours. If you are impacted by a power outage, SDG&E recommends visiting their website to get updates on restoration.
Hottest first pitch ever at Petco Park
Wednesday's temperatures broke the record of the hottest first pitch ever at Petco Park in downtown San Diego, according to the Padres baseball team.
Despite the extreme temperatures, the Friar Faithful still showed up in droves to support their team.
It was the hottest Padres game ever in Petco Park history. NBC 7's Jeanette Quezada has more on how fans tried to stay cool during the game.
Cooling off during the heat
The NWS issues these warnings because heat illnesses increase during periods of extreme heat. Residents are urged to drink plenty of fluids, stay in air-conditioned rooms and stay out of the sun.
San Diego County released tips and advisories on avoiding heat-related illnesses here.
Never leave pets or children unattended in vehicles. "Car interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes," the NWS said.
Dozens of locations across San Diego County act as "Cool Zones," providing a space where residents can seek relief from the heat for free. See the list here.
San Diegans and tourists packed local beaches this Labor Day to escape the sweltering heat and muggy conditions, reports NBC 7's Todd Strain.

articles.full_text:
Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed
OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Portsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol and Nottingham will be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research.
Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain. Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence.
Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas.
Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the least tree cover, green space and waterways.
This summer was provisionally the UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future.
The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth, Leicester and Exeter, according to the analysis.
Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives.
“Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.”
Portsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol and Brighton and Hove by the end of this century.
Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation.
The City of London and the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK.
The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth.
A study commissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services.
The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe.
Among cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces.
Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said.
“We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.”

articles.full_text:
It's official, Wednesday was the hottest day of 2026 everywhere. A record of 107 for San Luis Obispo
An extreme heat warning continues until 8 pm Thursday. It's official, Wednesday was the hottest day of 2026 everywhere. A record of 107 for San Luis Obispo and 96 in Santa Barbara
Hottest day of 2026 from Meteorologist Jim Castillo
CENTRAL COAST HEAT UPDATE
TEMPERATURE BREAKDOWN It's official, Wednesday was the hottest day of 2026 everywhere. A new daily record of 107 for San Luis Obispo. I had to go back to March when we hit 97 twice to find numbers this high. The high in Santa Barbara was 96 degrees. 106 in Paso Robles and Santa Ynez. Wednesday's peak temperatures reached the mid-90s to low 100s even at some beach locations and areas west of the mountains. Interior valleys saw temperatures between 100 and 108 degrees. Overnight lows offer little relief, staying in the 60s and 70s.
EXTREME HEAT PEAKED WEDNESDAY The most dangerous heat is behind us, but Thursday remains very hot across both San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties. High risk for heat illness continues, especially in interior valleys and foothills.
Isolated showers and thunderstorms developed Wednesday over the Los Padres National Forest. Activity was concentrated around the Cuyama Valley region. Brief downpours and lightning pushed in from Ventura County.
COASTAL CONCERNS IN SANTA BARBARA COUNTY Elevated surf and rip current risk will persist along Santa Barbara County beaches through Thursday evening. Wave heights of 3 to 5 feet with occasional 6-foot sets. Conditions improve Thursday afternoon as the south swell subsides.
Thursday brings 4 to 10 degrees of cooling west of the mountains as upper-level high pressure weakens slightly. Interior sections see minimal change. Extreme Heat Warnings remain in effect through Thursday evening.
WEEKEND RELIEF COMING Friday and Saturday show a more significant cooling trend. Onshore flow increases, marine layer clouds return to the coast, and temperatures drop 5 to 10 degrees below seasonal averages. Most areas will see highs in the 70s and 80s by Saturday.
WIND CONDITIONS Expect typical afternoon southwest winds of 15 to 25 mph across the Santa Lucia and Santa Ynez Mountains. Gusts to 35 mph possible along ridgelines. Coastal areas remain relatively calm with light onshore breezes.
The dangerous heat phase of this weather pattern concludes Thursday as a more typical marine influence returns to the Central Coast.

A low‑pressure area formed over the Bay of Bengal has triggered widespread rainfall alerts across Odisha, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) warning of heavy to extremely heavy showers in several districts.
On Thursday, Mayurbhanj district was placed under a red alert for very heavy rainfall, while other regions were cautioned about thunderstorms accompanied by lightning. Authorities ordered the closure of all government and aided schools in Mayurbhanj as a precautionary measure.
Meteorologists noted that the cyclonic circulation associated with the system extends up to 9.4 km in the atmosphere, tilting southwestward. Over the next three days, orange and yellow warnings have been issued for districts including Kalahandi, Nabarangpur, Koraput, and parts of southern and western Odisha.
The IMD forecast indicates that rainfall activity will continue till September 12, with intensity peaking in southern Odisha. From September 13 to 17, no warnings have been issued, suggesting a likely reduction in rainfall activity.
Officials urged residents to remain cautious, as heavy showers could lead to waterlogging and disruption of normal life in vulnerable areas.

In addition to a heat advisory this week, officials have issued a smog alert and are warning coastal residents of minor coastal flooding.
A Spare the Air alert has been issued for Wednesday by the Bay Area Air District, with concentrations of ozone expected to be unhealthy. Ozone is a reactive gas that acts as a protective shield against ultraviolet rays in the high atmosphere, but it forms harmful smog at ground level, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The Bay Area Air District reports the highest concentrations of ozone are in the Eastern Zone, which includes San Ramon and Fairfield, as well as the Santa Clara Valley.
The NWS has also extended its heat advisory through 10 p.m. Thursday. High temperatures in interior portions of the Bay Area will peak between 90 and 105 degrees and dip to the 70s at night. Coastal highs will be in the mid 70s to low 90s, with overnight lows mostly in the mid to high 60s.
Wednesday's afternoon high was expected to reach 98 degrees at Napa County Airport.
The weather service recommends limiting unnecessary outdoor activity to avoid heat illness, taking breaks in the shade and drinking cool water. Never leave children or pets in parked cars, or leave pets or livestock without shade and water.
Marin County issued a statement for residents to look for the warning signs of heat-related illness. Heat exhaustion occurs with symptoms that include thirst, weakness, muscle cramps, nausea, sweating and a rapid pulse. Heat stroke is the most serious heat injury and requires emergency treatment. Signs include confusion, altered sweating, hot, flushed or dry skin, nausea, vomiting, rapid breathing, racing heart rate and headache. Call 911 and cool the effected person while waiting for help.
The National Weather Service is forecasting the possibility of up to 1.2 feet of coastal flooding in low-lying areas near shorelines and waterways along the shoreline areas of San Francisco, San Pablo and Monterey bays. A minor coastal flooding alert is in effect through 1 a.m. Thursday. The highest tide is predicted to reach 5.7 feet above sea level at 11:30 p.m. on Wednesday.
Travelers are advised to take time to plan safer routes and to never drive through water of unknown depth.
